title: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: this phenomenon on its own can make no contribution at all to what we can reasonably consider the ultimate production of randomness.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Continuous Cellular Automata” (from p. 155), p. 155. Scope: chaotic dynamical systems and iterated maps

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-21: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specific mathematical readings can be analyzed using proofs and simulations, and counterexamples can separate sensitivity from chaotic mixing. The categorical conclusion depends on a contested definition of randomness production, so the claim as stated is not fully resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formalize production of randomness as growth in algorithmic or stochastic information conditional on the exact initial state, then compare maps with positive sensitivity but differing information generation. Exact deterministic dynamics can be proved not to create algorithmic information beyond the rule and initial state, while practical entropy notions yield different answers.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ultimate production of randomness is a philosophical rather than standard measurable quantity.

Sensitive dependence and entropy production are related but not identical.

Deterministic, finite-precision, and stochastic notions give different verdicts.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: On the shift map the claim is the digit identity already settled by proof: sensitive dependence displays digits that were in the seed. Extending the same moral to every chaotic system, including ones Wolfram thinks generate randomness intrinsically, requires a decomposition of randomness that the simulations do not force. Rivals who treat sensitive dependence as the source of randomness read the same orbits differently, so only the shift-map case is a clean test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For the shift map, use the digit-shift identity: sensitive dependence only reveals later digits of the seed. For maps that also look random from simple seeds, separate amplified seed differences from irregularity already present at the simple seed. The general claim is confirmed only if that separation can be made; it is refuted if some system produces irregular output from a simple seed with no sensitive dependence, or if sensitive dependence is shown to add new irregularity beyond the seed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Whether sensitive dependence 'produces' randomness depends on whether one describes the state by its size or by its digits.

The general principle covers all chaotic systems, while the clean argument is specific to digit shifts.
